chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shazaan, from Safwan ibn Yahya, who said:

'Abdullah ibn Sinan came to me and said, 'Do you have anything?' I said, 'Yes.' So I sent my son and gave him a dirham to buy meat and eggs with it. He said to me, 'Where did you send your son?' So I informed him. He said, 'Send him back, send him back! Do you have oil?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Bring it, for I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man is ruined who belittles to his brother what is present with him, and a man is ruined who belittles to his brother what he brings to him.'

key_terms.زَيْتٌ: Oil (specifically olive oil, a staple of hospitality)
key_terms.قَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ: What he brought or offered to him
key_terms.يَحْضُرُهُ: What is present or available with him

ai.seo_question: What does it mean to belittle a brother's offering according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia emphasis on *adab* (etiquette) in social interactions, specifically the importance of not diminishing the value of a host's generosity. Safwan ibn Yahya’s immediate compliance with 'Abdullah ibn Sinan’s request to include oil demonstrates the practical application of Imam al-Sadiq’s teaching that overlooking even minor provisions can lead to spiritual ruin (*halaaka*) due to perceived slight. It highlights the scholarly view that hospitality is a holistic act of respect, where the completeness of the offering reflects the sincerity of the giver.
